Mr. Lisandro, the ahua, who very kindly received us and has

Through life, through nature,

00:10:57,080 --> 00:11:02,200

00:11:02,200 --> 00:11:07,760

00:11:07,760 --> 00:11:15,600
el bosque durante once meses. A finales de julio 
de 1944, nueve meses después del levantamiento,  

120
00:11:15,600 --> 00:11:22,320
el Ejército Rojo liberó la ciudad de Chelm, 
situada a unos 50 km de Sobibor. Los soldados  

121
00:11:22,320 --> 00:11:28,360
soviéticos encontraron a Rosenfeld 2 meses 
después en un área cercana y poco después pidió  

122
00:11:28,360 --> 00:11:33,920
al comando soviético que lo enviara al frente. Sin 
embargo, los soviéticos dudaban de que realmente  

123
00:11:33,920 --> 00:11:39,440
hubiera sobrevivido a dos años de cautiverio. 
Después de una cuidadosa evaluación por parte  

124
00:11:39,440 --> 00:11:44,800
de la unidad de contrainteligencia soviética 
SMERSH, Simjon Rosenfeld fue enviado a luchar  

125
00:11:44,800 --> 00:11:50,720
en el 1er Frente Bielorruso. Participó en el cruce 
del río Vístula y durante la batalla por la ciudad  

126
00:11:50,720 --> 00:11:59,800
de Poznan en el invierno de 1944-1945, Simjon 
resultó gravemente herido. Estuvo a punto de que  

127
00:11:59,800 --> 00:12:05,520
le amputaran un miembro cuando un joven médico 
judío le aconsejó que rechazara la operación.

128
00:12:05,520 --> 00:12:09,960
Después de ser dado de alta del hospital, 
Rosenfeld fue considerado no apto para  

129
00:12:09,960 --> 00:12:14,400
el combate y fue enviado a Berlín como 
comandante de una unidad que custodiaba  

130
00:12:14,400 --> 00:12:19,640
los suministros de alimentos del ejército. 
Allí sería testigo del final de la guerra.  

131
00:12:19,640 --> 00:12:24,920
En una columna del Reichstag, el parlamento 
alemán, garabateó la siguiente inscripción:

00:12:24,920 --> 00:12:32,200
"Baranovichi-Sobibor-Berlín". En 1945, 
Rosenfeld recibió las medallas por sus

00:12:32,200 --> 00:12:39,000
servicios de combate y por su coraje y regresó

00:12:39,000 --> 00:12:45,560

00:12:51,120 --> 00:12:59,120

Yevgeniya. Se establecieron en la localidad  

137
00:12:59,120 --> 00:13:04,120
ucraniana de Gaivoron, donde Simjon trabajaba 
como director de un taller de fotografía.

138
00:13:04,120 --> 00:13:11,040
Criaron a dos hijos y siguieron a sus hijos a

00:13:11,040 --> 00:13:17,400
no fue lo suficientemente prominente en la 
Unión Soviética, en 1963, después de 20 años,  

140
00:13:17,400 --> 00:13:23,760
Simjon conoció a Aleksandr Pecherskii y otros 
supervivientes del levantamiento. Continuaron  

141
00:13:23,760 --> 00:13:30,160
reuniéndose hasta 1990, cuando Pecherskii 
murió y los Rosenfeld emigraron a Israel. 

142

Aunque los nazis enterraron todas las pruebas

"No puedo creer que hayan dado con

00:13:49,680 --> 00:13:54,880
el campo. Es difícil imaginar que quedara

00:13:54,880 --> 00:13:59,400

00:13:59,400 --> 00:14:05,240

Cuando Simjon Rosenfeld murió el 3 de junio de

Le cortaron una aleta para

PHILIP: Alimentábamos la

Los convictos de Alcatraz eran

00:07:01,160 --> 00:07:02,600
NARRADOR: En sus

Para ellos, la fascinación por

HOMBRE: No quiero

146
00:07:44,800 --> 00:07:50,760

00:07:50,760 --> 00:07:51,520

00:07:51,520 --> 00:07:56,540

00:07:56,540 --> 00:07:58,800

00:08:04,120 --> 00:08:05,400
El temor de los prisioneros

Para nadar hasta la costa, Coe

00:08:20,680 --> 00:08:23,820

NARRADOR: Están decididos y

Los dos trabajaron en el ala

161
00:08:32,440 --> 00:08:35,640

00:08:35,640 --> 00:08:37,480
En su interior, hallaron una 

163
00:08:37,480 --> 00:08:41,480

00:08:41,480 --> 00:08:43,280
Día tras días, aserraron las 

165
00:08:43,280 --> 00:08:47,400

167
00:08:48,560 --> 00:08:59,480
Cubrían su dedicado trabajo

168
00:08:59,480 --> 00:09:00,960
Hasta que en un día de diciembre 

169
00:09:00,960 --> 00:09:04,640

170
00:09:04,640 --> 00:09:08,640

a prueba de fugas.

171
00:09:08,640 --> 00:09:11,640
Cuando el guardia se retiró

172
00:09:11,640 --> 00:09:12,840

173
00:09:12,840 --> 00:09:18,280
Cole y Roe pusieron
manos a la obra de su fuga.

174
00:09:18,280 --> 00:09:21,840
Llegaron rápidamente a la
cerca que bordea la costa

175
00:09:21,840 --> 00:09:25,800

176
00:09:25,800 --> 00:09:29,360
Eran libres o eso creían.

177
00:09:33,880 --> 00:09:36,880
Llevaban latas de gas que
habían robado del edificio de 

178
00:09:36,880 --> 00:09:38,880

179
00:09:38,880 --> 00:09:44,520
Se zambulleron en
la gélida bahía.

180
00:09:44,520 --> 00:09:48,880
Y desaparecieron.

181
00:09:48,880 --> 00:09:52,520
Nunca más fueron vistos.

182
00:09:52,520 --> 00:09:54,120
Nadie sabe qué pasó, 

183

184
00:09:57,260 --> 00:10:00,720

NARRADOR: Además de las helads

189

190
00:10:12,840 --> 00:10:17,240
Ese día en particular, la niebla

191

00:10:20,960 --> 00:10:24,920
Desorientados por la niebla

196
00:10:31,040 --> 00:10:34,240
Pero algunos incluso los
prisioneros que permanecían 

197

198
00:10:37,360 --> 00:10:47,360
¿habrán sido devorados

199
00:10:47,360 --> 00:10:48,680
Hay casi una docena de 

200
00:10:48,680 --> 00:10:51,200

201
00:10:51,200 --> 00:10:54,120
Se los encuentra de
todo tamaño y forma

202
00:10:54,120 --> 00:10:57,320

203
00:10:57,320 --> 00:11:01,520
a los intimidantemente grandes

204
00:11:01,520 --> 00:11:04,120
A pesar de su gigantesco
tamaño, los tiburones 

205
00:11:04,120 --> 00:11:06,200

206
00:11:06,200 --> 00:11:09,840
Se alimentan filtrando el
agua con sus branquias.

207
00:11:09,840 --> 00:11:11,320
Pero hay un tiburón que 

208
00:11:11,320 --> 00:11:15,600

que podría ser peligroso

209
00:11:15,600 --> 00:11:17,960
tiburón vaca de hocico corto.

210
00:11:17,960 --> 00:11:21,280
DOUGLAS: Los tiburones vaca
pueden llegar a medir hasta 

211
00:11:21,280 --> 00:11:23,400

00:11:23,400 --> 00:11:28,240

00:11:28,240 --> 00:11:29,920
Se sabe que forman grupos

215
00:11:34,240 --> 00:11:35,680
Pero hasta la fecha no se 

216

217
00:11:39,560 --> 00:11:41,900

218
00:11:41,900 --> 00:11:45,760
NARRADOR: De hecho, ninguna

219
00:11:45,760 --> 00:11:46,960

00:11:46,960 --> 00:11:51,160

221
00:11:51,160 --> 00:11:55,480
Ecxepto uno el tiburón blanco.

222
00:11:55,480 --> 00:11:59,480
DOUGLAS: Son tiburones
que pesan 1500 kilos y tienen 

223

224
00:12:02,720 --> 00:12:05,640
Pueden cortar a la mitad a un

225
00:12:05,640 --> 00:12:08,920
Pueden destripar a un

226
00:12:08,920 --> 00:12:13,700
Y, una vez que está

227
00:12:13,700 --> 00:12:17,040
NARRADOR: Evolucionaron a lo

228
00:12:17,040 --> 00:12:20,360

229
00:12:20,360 --> 00:12:24,880
Sus afilados dientes se

230
00:12:24,880 --> 00:12:26,400
Tienen órganos sensoriales 

231
00:12:26,400 --> 00:12:28,700

232
00:12:28,700 --> 00:12:33,520

233
00:12:33,520 --> 00:12:39,760
Y una estrategia letal el

234
00:12:39,760 --> 00:12:42,320
Una vez que el tiburón
blanco eligió a su presa

235
00:12:42,320 --> 00:12:44,920

236
00:12:44,920 --> 00:12:48,080
SCOTT: Si estás en el agua

él te verá a ti y tú
nunca a él.

238
00:12:53,950 --> 00:12:57,320
NARRADOR: Aunque los
tiburones blancos casi

241
00:13:02,680 --> 00:13:06,000
En 1959, un impactante encuentro

243
00:13:08,640 --> 00:13:13,920

244
00:13:13,920 --> 00:13:16,960

245
00:13:16,960 --> 00:13:20,000
Fue un ataque brutal

246
00:13:20,000 --> 00:13:29,160

247
00:13:29,160 --> 00:13:31,960
Mayo de 1959.

248
00:13:31,960 --> 00:13:34,400
San Francisco, California.

249
00:13:34,400 --> 00:13:38,160
Es una tarde calurosa, soleada
en la playa Baker, una hermosa 

250
00:13:38,160 --> 00:13:39,120
extensión de arena

251
00:13:39,120 --> 00:13:41,080
a pocos metros de la bahía

252
00:13:41,080 --> 00:13:42,400
a menos de un kilómetro 

253
00:13:42,400 --> 00:13:46,640
y medio al sudoeste
del puente Golden Gate.

254
00:13:46,640 --> 00:13:48,440
Shirley O'Neill y Albert 

255
00:13:48,440 --> 00:13:52,000
Kogler eran dos estudiantes
universitarios de 18 años

256
00:13:52,000 --> 00:13:52,840
que habían venido a 

257
00:13:52,840 --> 00:13:56,880

larga semana de clases.

258
00:13:56,880 --> 00:14:03,120
La pareja se sumerge en

259
00:14:03,120 --> 00:14:10,880
El día no podría

260
00:14:10,880 --> 00:14:15,080
Pero todo está por cambiar.

261
00:14:15,080 --> 00:14:16,520
Pasan la primera rompiente 

262
00:14:16,520 --> 00:14:21,600

profundas, más tranquilas.

263
00:14:21,600 --> 00:14:26,960
Mientras Albert mira
hacia el horizonte,

264
00:14:26,960 --> 00:14:30,600
Shirley ve pasar una gigantesa
sombra a pocos metros de la 

265
00:14:30,600 --> 00:14:34,720

266
00:14:34,720 --> 00:14:42,120

directamente hacia él.

267
00:14:42,120 --> 00:14:44,160
El agua entra en ebullición.

268
00:14:44,160 --> 00:14:50,320
Es un tiburón gigantesco de casi
5 metros de largo que entierra 

269
00:14:50,320 --> 00:14:53,220

270
00:14:53,220 --> 00:14:54,800

271
00:14:54,800 --> 00:14:59,520
Los instintos de Shirley le

272
00:14:59,520 --> 00:15:03,880

273
00:15:03,880 --> 00:15:10,160
El tiburón vuelve a morderlo

274

Lo toma del torso y, haciendo

275

276
00:15:19,860 --> 00:15:24,600

277
00:15:24,600 --> 00:15:27,880

278

279

280
00:15:34,140 --> 00:15:36,240

281
00:15:36,240 --> 00:15:38,040

283
00:15:45,000 --> 00:15:48,240

284
00:15:48,240 --> 00:15:49,760
El mortífero ataque

285

286
00:15:54,240 --> 00:15:56,880
SCOTT: Albert Kogler murió tras 

287
00:15:56,880 --> 00:16:00,760

288
00:16:00,760 --> 00:16:02,560
Miren hacia allí y miren 

289
00:16:02,560 --> 00:16:05,760

290
00:16:05,760 --> 00:16:08,200
NARRADOR: Sin embargo, y pesea 

291

292

293
00:16:15,120 --> 00:16:18,000

294
00:16:18,000 --> 00:16:19,920
¿Por qué? Porque la bahía es 

295
00:16:19,920 --> 00:16:23,520

296
00:16:23,520 --> 00:16:24,600

297
00:16:24,600 --> 00:16:27,800

marea sube, y de agua dulce,

298
00:16:27,800 --> 00:16:30,800

bahía de los ríos.

299
00:16:30,800 --> 00:16:31,720
Se sabe que el agua 

300
00:16:31,720 --> 00:16:34,840

301
00:16:34,840 --> 00:16:36,500

302
00:16:36,500 --> 00:16:38,080
DOUGLAS: ¿Qué pasaría si los 

303
00:16:38,080 --> 00:16:41,080

304
00:16:41,080 --> 00:16:43,040

305
00:16:43,040 --> 00:16:45,200
Están acostumbrados a un entorno 

306
00:16:45,200 --> 00:16:48,840

eso se reduciría su capacidad

307
00:16:48,840 --> 00:16:49,920
de reacción, sus 

308
00:16:49,920 --> 00:16:52,600
estructuras sensoriales
no funcionarían tan bien,

309
00:16:52,600 --> 00:16:55,440
disminuiría su capacidad
para nadar, sus órganos 

310
00:16:55,440 --> 00:16:57,160

311
00:16:57,160 --> 00:16:59,840
descompensaciones que con el
tiempo les causarían la muerte.

312
00:16:59,840 --> 00:17:05,040
Fisiológicamente, no soportarían
estar en un entorno poco salino.

313
00:17:05,040 --> 00:17:09,040
NARRADOR: Pero en 2007 y 2008, 

314
00:17:09,040 --> 00:17:12,360

de la universidad de Stanford

315
00:17:12,360 --> 00:17:15,680
sobre la migración de los
tiburones blancos, los sensors 

316
00:17:15,680 --> 00:17:16,760

317
00:17:16,760 --> 00:17:18,720

318
00:17:18,720 --> 00:17:24,360

319
00:17:24,360 --> 00:17:27,040
Si bien contaban con pruebas
de que a veces los tiburones

00:17:27,040 --> 00:17:28,960
blancos ingresaban a la bahía,

321
00:17:28,960 --> 00:17:31,680
hasta hace poco la mayoría de
los expertos creían que las 

322
00:17:31,680 --> 00:17:33,360

323
00:17:33,360 --> 00:17:35,760
para que los tiburones
blancos lograran cazar.

324
00:17:35,760 --> 00:17:39,120
Las mareas arrastran algas y
sedimentos y la visibilidad en 

325
00:17:39,120 --> 00:17:42,640

Sharks off the coast of the Carolinas attacked

7
00:00:25,488 --> 00:00:29,325
unexpectedly to 11 people.

8
00:00:29,425 --> 00:00:30,994
WOMAN: True. MAN: Tore off his arm.

9
00:00:32,595 --> 00:00:34,897
NARRATOR: While the attacks were making headlines.

10
00:00:34,998 --> 00:00:38,068
WOMAN: You don't see anyone swimming these days!

11
00:00:38,168 --> 00:00:43,640
NARRATOR: Experts are wondering: What's causing this sudden outbreak?

12
00:00:43,740 --> 00:00:48,145
GREG: There must be something that triggers it.

13
00:00:48,245 --> 00:00:52,649
NARRATOR: Now, two scientists from totally different worlds

14
00:00:52,749 --> 00:00:55,918
They look for the answer.

15
00:00:56,019 --> 00:01:00,423
They dive into waters full of sharks.

16
00:01:00,523 --> 00:01:03,426
JOE: You guys are completely crazy!

17
00:01:03,526 --> 00:01:07,697
NARRATOR: To test his revolutionary theory.

18
00:01:07,797 --> 00:01:10,967
GREG: He's coming so fast! He's fast!

19
00:01:11,067 --> 00:01:14,905
NARRATOR: Such attacks could be weather-related.

20
00:01:19,108 --> 00:01:24,413
If true, it could change our knowledge about sharks and rides.

21
00:01:24,513 --> 00:01:27,184
on the beach, forever.

22
00:01:36,692 --> 00:01:37,994
The Bahamas.

23
00:01:40,197 --> 00:01:43,532
Join a veteran shark scientist.

24
00:01:43,633 --> 00:01:46,502
GREG: If we can use the weather to indicate what sharks do,

25
00:01:46,602 --> 00:01:49,305
We could predict whether a shark attack will happen or not!

26
00:01:49,405 --> 00:01:52,075
And that would be wonderful!

27
00:01:52,175 --> 00:01:55,078
NARRATOR: And a very experienced meteorologist.

28
00:01:55,178 --> 00:01:59,616
JOE: I'm excited to work with Greg and show him that my hypothesis is correct:

29
00:01:59,716 --> 00:02:05,355
that wind and weather have an effect on where sharks are located.

30
00:02:06,456 --> 00:02:09,526
NARRATOR: And you might discover something very important.

31
00:02:12,995 --> 00:02:17,900
It may sound crazy that the weather can help predict the likelihood of an attack.

32
00:02:18,000 --> 00:02:23,807
of shark, but the science behind the theory is real.

33
00:02:25,641 --> 00:02:29,512
JOE: My name is Joe Merchant, I'm a meteorologist with the National Weather Service.

34
00:02:29,613 --> 00:02:32,448
My goal is to protect lives and property.

35
00:02:32,548 --> 00:02:37,687
I am trained to deal with storm warnings and hurricane watch,

36
00:02:37,787 --> 00:02:40,389
hurricane warnings, including tornado warnings.

37
00:02:40,490 --> 00:02:44,260
I've actually had to chase tornadoes.

38
00:02:44,360 --> 00:02:47,930
Look at that!

39
00:02:48,030 --> 00:02:51,200
NARRATOR: Sharks weren't part of Joe's forecast.

40
00:02:51,300 --> 00:02:56,406
until the tsunami of attacks in 2015 caught their attention.

41
00:02:58,942 --> 00:03:02,879
JOE: There were 11 shark attacks off the coast of the Carolinas.

42
00:03:02,979 --> 00:03:05,214
There I began to observe the weather.

43
00:03:05,314 --> 00:03:13,089
I observed the weather during these attacks and saw that there was a pattern.

44
00:03:13,189 --> 00:03:18,094
I decided to call the only shark expert I had read about: Dr. Skomal.

45
00:03:18,194 --> 00:03:19,996
GREG: My name is Greg Skomal, I'm a biologist.

46
00:03:20,096 --> 00:03:23,199
And affiliated with the Massachusetts Division of Marine Fisheries.

47
00:03:23,299 --> 00:03:26,068
I have studied sharks for over 30 years.

48
00:03:26,168 --> 00:03:29,939
I have focused especially on the great white shark.

49
00:03:30,039 --> 00:03:32,208
When Joes called me I had all these ideas about

50
00:03:32,308 --> 00:03:35,044
how climate change patterns might influence

51
00:03:35,145 --> 00:03:37,347
to an animal that lives in the water.

52
00:03:37,447 --> 00:03:40,750
It started to make a little sense.

53
00:03:40,850 --> 00:03:47,857
NARRATOR: Now, Joe teams up with Greg to test his bold new theory.

54
00:03:47,957 --> 00:03:54,096
Joe believes that the winds attract small marine life closer to the shore.

55
00:03:54,196 --> 00:03:59,635
These small prey attract large predators.

56
00:03:59,735 --> 00:04:05,108
Which in turn attracts the largest predators: sharks.

57
00:04:05,208 --> 00:04:08,144
Follow this food chain that the wind brings,

58
00:04:08,244 --> 00:04:14,483
This is what drives sharks towards the shore, close to swimmers.

59
00:04:14,583 --> 00:04:18,054
JOE: Taking what we know from the wind forecast,

60
00:04:18,154 --> 00:04:21,624
We can use this information and put it into a model

61
00:04:21,724 --> 00:04:26,729
and thus predict where a shark attack might occur.

62
00:04:26,829 --> 00:04:32,368
So that on a Sunday afternoon, if a family goes to the beach,

63
00:04:32,468 --> 00:04:38,474
can have a very clear idea of where the sharks are.

64
00:04:38,575 --> 00:04:43,446
NARRATOR: To test Joe's theory they want to observe two different species,

65
00:04:43,546 --> 00:04:50,619
frequently involved in human attacks: tiger sharks, and bull sharks.

66
00:04:50,720 --> 00:04:54,891
There are many of them here in the Bahamas.

67
00:04:54,991 --> 00:04:56,960
First, the tigers.

68
00:04:57,060 --> 00:04:58,427
GREG: Here we go!

69
00:04:58,527 --> 00:05:01,230
Joe, we'll head towards Tiger Beach, which is up here. JOE: Okay.

70
00:05:01,330 --> 00:05:03,132
GREG: Yeah, right at the edge of this bench.

71
00:05:03,232 --> 00:05:07,503
Uh, very deep water to the west, shallow water to the east,

72
00:05:07,603 --> 00:05:12,975
and there are lots of tiger sharks here.

73
00:05:13,075 --> 00:05:17,180
NARRATOR: Their mission: to tag sharks with tracking devices.

74
00:05:17,280 --> 00:05:22,919
to observe whether they respond to the changing climate.

75
00:05:23,019 --> 00:05:25,322
But it won't be easy.

76
00:05:28,958 --> 00:05:34,631
Tiger sharks are some of the most formidable hunters in the ocean.

77
00:05:34,731 --> 00:05:38,101
Predators with large, flat noses that can measure up to

78
00:05:38,201 --> 00:05:42,305
more than 5 meters and weigh almost a ton.

79
00:05:45,008 --> 00:05:49,178
Tiger sharks are named for their dark vertical lines.

80
00:05:49,278 --> 00:05:55,251
And they project their colors across the tropical and subtropical waters of the world.

81
00:05:56,318 --> 00:06:01,691
They have an almost limitless diet, ranging from natural prey, such as fish,

82
00:06:01,791 --> 00:06:03,493
seals and birds.

83
00:06:05,261 --> 00:06:10,699
Even human waste, such as car license plates and tires.

84
00:06:10,799 --> 00:06:17,507
This undiscerning palate sometimes also includes people.

85
00:06:17,607 --> 00:06:22,412
Leaving them second only to great white sharks in human attacks.

86
00:06:26,115 --> 00:06:29,218
And the perfect species to test the theory

87
00:06:29,318 --> 00:06:33,689
Joe's claim that wind plays a role in attacks.

88
00:06:33,790 --> 00:06:35,391
CAPTAIN: We're here, we need to anchor here.

89
00:06:35,491 --> 00:06:36,559
WOMAN: Understood.

90
00:06:52,641 --> 00:06:54,944
JOE: I've never seen a tiger shark before.

91
00:06:55,044 --> 00:06:57,213
And this is incredible.

92
00:06:57,313 --> 00:07:00,783
I think you can see my arm bristling right now.

93
00:07:00,883 --> 00:07:03,619
I'll definitely let Greg take it from here.

94
00:07:03,719 --> 00:07:09,992
I think I'll be watching the weather on the boat.

95
00:07:10,092 --> 00:07:11,761
I don't want to let go!

96
00:07:12,629 --> 00:07:15,798
GREG: Yeah, this is a good place.

97
00:07:15,898 --> 00:07:20,403
Without sharks you can't study them, so step one, complete!

98
00:07:20,503 --> 00:07:22,638
JOE: Yes. GREG: I like it.

99
00:07:22,738 --> 00:07:27,610
NARRATOR: Step two: Greg gets into the water with the tiger sharks.

100
00:07:27,710 --> 00:07:33,116
and mark them with monitoring equipment.

101
00:07:33,216 --> 00:07:36,686
GREG: We're going to attach this camera system to the shark's fin.

102
00:07:36,786 --> 00:07:40,823
It's a device that has all kinds of instrumentation in there,

103
00:07:40,923 --> 00:07:43,393
that measures temperature and depth.

104
00:07:43,493 --> 00:07:46,729
And it also has a camera system, so we can get a look

105
00:07:46,829 --> 00:07:49,199
of the shark about what is happening underwater.

106
00:07:49,299 --> 00:07:53,636
And the other instruments on it indicate the 3 movements of the shark

107
00:07:53,736 --> 00:07:57,673
to be able to know where it is going, how fast it is moving,

108
00:07:57,773 --> 00:08:02,144
up and down in the water column, in relation to temperature and depth.

109
00:08:02,244 --> 00:08:06,115
We will be able to correlate this behavior with the weather as it changes.

110
00:08:06,215 --> 00:08:08,550
and the wind increases, we will know what the shark is doing

111
00:08:08,650 --> 00:08:10,954
in relation to climate changes.

112
00:08:11,054 --> 00:08:15,190
The key will be to slide it over the dorsal fin, right here.

113
00:08:15,291 --> 00:08:20,897
Let's pull the trigger, bang! We're going.

114
00:08:20,997 --> 00:08:23,932
It won't hurt the shark, it just holds onto the fin,

115
00:08:24,032 --> 00:08:26,001
I bet he won't even react.

116
00:08:26,101 --> 00:08:29,739
It sounds easy, but I have to get as close as I can, then align it,

117
00:08:29,839 --> 00:08:31,341
and wait for him to cooperate.

118
00:08:31,441 --> 00:08:34,843
Many things have to turn out excellent.

119
00:08:34,943 --> 00:08:39,248
NARRATOR: Tigers aren't the only predators in these waters.

120
00:08:39,349 --> 00:08:45,320
Bull and lemon sharks are never far away.

121
00:08:45,421 --> 00:08:48,558
Especially when it's mealtime.

122
00:08:49,225 --> 00:08:54,329
GRANT: We have so many sharks here that we have to try to keep them

123
00:08:54,429 --> 00:08:56,599
a little far from us.

124
00:08:57,333 --> 00:09:00,736
When you have so many sharks in the same area,

125
00:09:00,836 --> 00:09:02,405
they start competing with each other.

126
00:09:11,948 --> 00:09:15,752
NARRATOR: The team is racing against the clock to complete their mission:

127
00:09:17,219 --> 00:09:19,756
a storm is approaching the islands.

128
00:09:22,325 --> 00:09:27,296
JOE: We're starting to see a little bit of instability thanks to that big storm.

129
00:09:27,396 --> 00:09:32,068
It's a sign that things are going to change here very soon.

130
00:09:32,168 --> 00:09:37,006
NARRATOR: Joe thinks the storm will hit tomorrow afternoon.

131
00:09:37,106 --> 00:09:42,178
JOE: The faster you get in the water and tag a shark, the better.

132
00:09:42,278 --> 00:09:47,850
And we'll be able to see how the shark reacts to the storm system.

133
00:09:52,688 --> 00:09:54,723
You guys are completely crazy!

134
00:09:54,823 --> 00:09:56,793
GREG: All right, I'm going after them!

135
00:10:10,439 --> 00:10:13,676
NARRATOR: The lemon sharks arrive immediately.

136
00:10:16,479 --> 00:10:19,048
It's a shark storm.

137
00:10:44,374 --> 00:10:47,076
JOE: Okay, now I'm going to put this in.

138
00:10:50,613 --> 00:10:53,983
Testing: one, two, three.

139
00:10:54,083 --> 00:10:58,053
I wanted to check that you were okay down there.

140
00:10:58,153 --> 00:11:01,724
GREG: I'm fine, Joe.

141
00:11:01,824 --> 00:11:03,559
JOE: Tell me what you're watching?

142
00:11:07,630 --> 00:11:10,099
GREG: I see a tiger! I see a tiger!

143
00:11:14,136 --> 00:11:18,541
NARRATOR: Now, Greg needs to get close enough to tag him.

144
00:11:37,693 --> 00:11:39,629
JOE: Greg? This is Joe, can you hear me?

145
00:11:42,865 --> 00:11:44,167
I don't hear anything.

146
00:11:46,535 --> 00:11:49,038
GREG: He's coming very fast! Very fast!

147
00:11:53,242 --> 00:11:55,011
I'm having a hard time marking it.

148
00:12:02,484 --> 00:12:03,986
Let's go. Let's go.

149
00:12:08,958 --> 00:12:11,994
GREG: I see a tiger! I see a tiger!

150
00:12:14,363 --> 00:12:16,732
I'm having a hard time marking it.

151
00:12:18,100 --> 00:12:22,705
NARRATOR: Shark biologist Greg Skomal and meteorologist Joe Merchant,

152
00:12:22,805 --> 00:12:26,141
They try to test a new revolutionary theory

153
00:12:26,241 --> 00:12:29,778
which could help predict shark attacks:

154
00:12:29,878 --> 00:12:33,816
They believe that sharks react to the weather, and that certain winds can

155
00:12:33,916 --> 00:12:37,920
take sharks to hunt near the coast,

156
00:12:38,020 --> 00:12:43,292
which causes shark attacks on swimmers.

157
00:12:43,392 --> 00:12:45,861
JOE: There are many!

158
00:12:45,961 --> 00:12:49,865
GREG: We look forward to seeing how changes in the climate above the water influence

159
00:12:49,965 --> 00:12:52,201
in the behavior of sharks underwater.

160
00:12:56,104 --> 00:12:59,942
NARRATOR: Greg must first tie up a complex system of cameras and computers

161
00:13:00,042 --> 00:13:03,846
to the dorsal fin of one of these tiger sharks.

162
00:13:09,218 --> 00:13:12,722
The forecast down here is for high pressure.

163
00:13:14,123 --> 00:13:15,758
Blood pressure.

164
00:13:20,930 --> 00:13:23,099
GREG: He's got Grant's fin!

165
00:13:28,303 --> 00:13:30,306
He's got Grant's dive bag!

166
00:13:33,676 --> 00:13:36,512
Oh no, he's attacking the bait box!

167
00:13:36,612 --> 00:13:42,651
NARRATOR: Then another aggressive species approaches and takes action.

168
00:13:42,751 --> 00:13:46,556
GREG: Oh, a hammerhead shark appeared out of nowhere!

169
00:13:52,761 --> 00:13:56,532
JOE: Greg, there are a lot of sharks swimming around you!

170
00:14:00,035 --> 00:14:02,071
GREG: There's complete chaos here!

171
00:14:02,171 --> 00:14:15,318
(music)

172
00:14:15,418 --> 00:14:17,052
Damn!

173
00:14:17,152 --> 00:14:21,991
(music)

174
00:14:22,091 --> 00:14:23,960
There are too many! Let's go up!

175
00:14:34,036 --> 00:14:38,807
NARRATOR: Greg's first attempt to tag a shark was too dangerous.

176
00:14:38,907 --> 00:14:40,942
JOE: Did you make it? GREG: No. They were

177
00:14:41,043 --> 00:14:46,615
JOE: No? GREG: Damn!

178
00:14:46,715 --> 00:14:55,390
It's frustrating! We came close, three or four times.

179
00:14:55,491 --> 00:14:57,326
GRANT: That tiger shark came really close!

180
00:14:57,426 --> 00:14:59,462
As soon as that bait went down to the bottom!

181
00:15:02,565 --> 00:15:04,666
GREG: You were the most popular guy on campus!

182
00:15:04,766 --> 00:15:10,206
GRANT: Yeah, they were a little too close for my liking.

183
00:15:10,306 --> 00:15:13,275
JOE: At one point, it seemed like some of the other sharks

184
00:15:13,375 --> 00:15:14,510
they were getting in each other's way a little.

185
00:15:18,847 --> 00:15:23,119
GREG: The hammerhead shark kept getting in the way.

186
00:15:23,219 --> 00:15:25,288
I never thought there would be so many sharks.

187
00:15:29,658 --> 00:15:33,696
We have to get in there and try again. JOE: Okay.

188
00:15:40,202 --> 00:15:43,806
I hope we can tag the shark very quickly.

189
00:15:43,906 --> 00:15:46,542
because that great storm is approaching,

190
00:15:46,642 --> 00:15:52,481
These are the conditions I would have expected for a shark attack.

191
00:15:52,581 --> 00:15:56,185
NARRATOR: Joe anticipates the storm will bring winds similar to those

192
00:15:56,285 --> 00:16:02,924
that occurred during the spate of attacks in the Carolinas in 2015.

193
00:16:03,024 --> 00:16:05,528
JOE: Greg, they're coming in!

194
00:16:15,671 --> 00:16:18,040
GREG: The tiger is coming!

195
00:16:25,214 --> 00:16:26,949
I'll try to mark it!

196
00:16:32,220 --> 00:16:34,390
Come here, come here!

197
00:16:43,632 --> 00:16:47,870
I got it! I did it! Finally! Yuhuuu.

198
00:17:01,250 --> 00:17:04,253
JOE: They did it! They did it! Good!

199
00:17:05,487 --> 00:17:07,289
(laughs)

200
00:17:13,428 --> 00:17:14,964
Genial.

201
00:17:20,403 --> 00:17:22,771
GREG: Yeah, we got one! GRANT: Yeah?

202
00:17:22,871 --> 00:17:26,909
GREG: We were late. One finally came over, behaved himself.

203
00:17:27,009 --> 00:17:30,780
We tried, the clamp got stuck.

204
00:17:30,880 --> 00:17:33,916
Then we came back, tried again, bang!

205
00:17:34,016 --> 00:17:36,685
We did it, great it was great.

206
00:17:36,785 --> 00:17:39,821
JOE: Excellent! GREG: Yes.

207
00:17:39,921 --> 00:17:44,860
Now the experiment begins! It's what we wanted.

208
00:17:44,960 --> 00:17:49,198
NARRATOR: All thanks to the tiger's new gadget.

209
00:17:49,298 --> 00:17:53,735
JOE: It means we're now going to be able to combine this new information with the weather data.

210
00:17:53,835 --> 00:17:59,241
And let's hope we see exactly what I think is happening:

211
00:17:59,341 --> 00:18:02,111
that the weather may be playing a role in the events

212
00:18:02,211 --> 00:18:08,117
that lead to those shark attacks.

213
00:18:08,217 --> 00:18:12,121
GREG: Every second it's collecting dozens of data points.

214
00:18:12,221 --> 00:18:14,390
JOE: Right.

215
00:18:14,490 --> 00:18:18,727
GREG: So the more seconds you're out, minutes, hours,

216
00:18:18,827 --> 00:18:20,362
we will get more information.

217
00:18:23,465 --> 00:18:25,200
But we have to get it back!

218
00:18:25,300 --> 00:18:26,802
That's the key!

219
00:18:37,179 --> 00:18:40,349
Having tagged the shark is the first step.

220
00:18:40,449 --> 00:18:43,518
Collecting data and literally collecting

221
00:18:43,618 --> 00:18:46,421
thousands of information points every minute,

222
00:18:46,522 --> 00:18:51,327
We will get a lot of this research, but only if we recover it.

223
00:18:52,728 --> 00:18:56,398
These are sharks capable of swimming hundreds of kilometers.

224
00:18:56,498 --> 00:18:59,701
And it is also a very big ocean.

225
00:18:59,801 --> 00:19:01,837
NARRATOR: The tiger shark's apparatus will take off

226
00:19:01,937 --> 00:19:06,174
in about 5 hours and will float to the surface.

227
00:19:06,274 --> 00:19:12,647
This is when the device's light will activate, allowing the team to track it.

228
00:19:12,747 --> 00:19:15,784
GREG: It could be 3 meters away or 32 kilometers away.

229
00:19:15,884 --> 00:19:20,422
So we need to make sure that all the technology takes us to the right place.

230
00:19:20,522 --> 00:19:23,392
We have to locate it using satellite receivers

231
00:19:23,492 --> 00:19:24,793
and high frequency.

232
00:19:24,893 --> 00:19:29,964
But there is always the possibility of never finding it.

233
00:19:30,065 --> 00:19:33,569
NARRATOR: Especially with the storm that's about to hit Tiger Beach soon.

234
00:19:44,179 --> 00:19:46,848
GREG: The longer he stays with the fish, the more information we'll have.

235
00:19:46,948 --> 00:19:48,350
It's very exciting.

236
00:19:48,450 --> 00:19:50,786
We have the shark swimming in the sea,

237
00:19:50,886 --> 00:19:54,122
He has the data collector and camera on his back!

238
00:19:54,223 --> 00:19:57,425
I think we should come here every hour, during the night.

239
00:19:57,525 --> 00:20:03,832
It should emerge in 4 or 5 hours, so we have time, but I want to see it.

240
00:20:08,537 --> 00:20:12,140
NARRATOR: The new dawn shows no sign of the device,

241
00:20:12,240 --> 00:20:15,243
but reveals a growing threat.

242
00:20:15,343 --> 00:20:18,313
JOE: It's a funnel cloud. That one over there is.

243
00:20:18,413 --> 00:20:22,017
It's a sign that things are changing now.

244
00:20:22,117 --> 00:20:26,755
NARRATOR: The storm Joe predicted is heading straight for them.

245
00:20:26,855 --> 00:20:30,725
JOE: You can see all those clouds gathering over there.

246
00:20:30,825 --> 00:20:32,494
GREG: It's raining a lot! JOE: Yes.

247
00:20:32,594 --> 00:20:36,365
So this is the beginning of the end of our time on the boat.

248
00:20:37,866 --> 00:20:39,301
GREG: That's very disturbing!

00:38:10,851 --> 00:38:12,319
GREG: Tell me, what color is it?

492
00:38:12,419 --> 00:38:15,956
JOE: It's actually grayer. Not as brown as cats. You know what I mean?

493
00:38:16,056 --> 00:38:19,127
GREG: Really? Is it big? JOE: Yeah, it's big!

494
00:38:19,227 --> 00:38:20,461
GREG: Really?

495
00:38:20,561 --> 00:38:22,229
Well, bring the device and the pole.

496
00:38:22,329 --> 00:38:23,564
JOE: All right.

497
00:38:23,664 --> 00:38:25,432
You'll definitely be able to score this one, Greg.

498
00:38:25,532 --> 00:38:26,868
GREG: Are you serious?

499
00:38:26,968 --> 00:38:29,203
JOE: Still, he's hanging around here.

500
00:38:29,303 --> 00:38:31,939
GREG: Joe Merch, attention. Ready for action.

501
00:38:34,442 --> 00:38:38,379
It could be a bull shark. That's what we wanted. See how it moves?

502
00:38:38,479 --> 00:38:40,414
Totally different. JOE: Yes.

503
00:38:40,514 --> 00:38:42,683
GREG: Oh my god, I'll have to go down and try that.

504
00:38:42,783 --> 00:38:44,085
It's not going to be easy. JOE: Can you do it?

505
00:38:46,120 --> 00:38:48,556
GREG: All right, Joe! Let's go. JOE: Are you okay?

506
00:38:48,656 --> 00:38:49,891
Okay. Watch out.

507
00:38:52,593 --> 00:38:55,830
GREG: You have to be patient.

508
00:38:55,930 --> 00:38:58,765
Okay, I'll try it now.

509
00:38:58,865 --> 00:39:02,003
Here it comes, coming closer, there it is. Let's go.

510
00:39:08,475 --> 00:39:10,344
JOE: Are you okay? Okay.

511
00:39:10,444 --> 00:39:12,079
GREG: I'm going to try it now.

512
00:39:12,179 --> 00:39:16,851
Here it comes, it's coming.

513
00:39:16,951 --> 00:39:17,852
I did it. JOE: Did you do it?

514
00:39:17,952 --> 00:39:19,820
GREG: Yes. I did.

515
00:39:19,920 --> 00:39:21,855
(laughs)

516
00:39:21,955 --> 00:39:23,157
I have it.

517
00:39:23,257 --> 00:39:24,958
JOE: I don't think so.

518
00:39:25,058 --> 00:39:26,027
GREG: beautiful.

519
00:39:31,531 --> 00:39:34,001
JOE: He turned left, you can't see it anymore.

520
00:39:34,102 --> 00:39:39,907
GREG: Well, maybe it's just coming out of the port, and I think that's great.

521
00:39:40,007 --> 00:39:41,409
Good! Great!

522
00:39:42,843 --> 00:39:44,278
Now we have to wait.

523
00:39:47,748 --> 00:39:51,886
We've been working here for 3 days and nothing, nothing, nothing.

524
00:39:51,986 --> 00:39:53,587
And suddenly, boom!

525
00:39:53,688 --> 00:39:57,324
Now we can start this experiment!

526
00:39:57,424 --> 00:40:01,462
JOE: We put the device on the bull and if it can stay on the shark,

527
00:40:01,562 --> 00:40:04,332
then we will get a large data set.

528
00:40:10,637 --> 00:40:14,642
NARRATOR: They have all the elements they need to prove their theory,

529
00:40:14,742 --> 00:40:18,745
that the wind affects the shark's behavior.

530
00:40:18,846 --> 00:40:26,520
A device on a bull shark and a strong northwest wind.

531
00:40:26,620 --> 00:40:30,691
JOE: I really hope we can get the device back from the bull shark because everything

532
00:40:30,791 --> 00:40:37,732
what I believe leads to a shark attack is happening right now.

533
00:40:37,832 --> 00:40:42,736
NARRATOR: Two and a half hours later, the device detaches itself from the bull shark.

534
00:40:42,836 --> 00:40:44,771
and they go in search of action.

535
00:40:44,871 --> 00:40:46,007
GREG: At 11 o'clock!

536
00:40:48,342 --> 00:40:50,511
Here we go! Perfect! We got it!

537
00:40:53,114 --> 00:40:58,519
NARRATOR: They return to the lab to analyze the information and material.

538
00:40:58,619 --> 00:41:03,390
JOE: If we can see the changes in the weather from below

539
00:41:03,490 --> 00:41:08,563
of the surface with the camera, then we could truly see,

540
00:41:08,663 --> 00:41:12,866
in real time the change in behavior of a shark.

541
00:41:12,966 --> 00:41:16,070
GREG: I'm excited to see this!

542
00:41:16,170 --> 00:41:20,775
I have the data and the videos here. Okay.

543
00:41:20,875 --> 00:41:24,712
JOE: I've been looking at the satellite and radar information from when we marked

544
00:41:24,812 --> 00:41:30,017
to the shark and you can see that it's a nice breezy day.

545
00:41:30,117 --> 00:41:31,685
GREG: Everything appears immediately.

546
00:41:31,785 --> 00:41:32,620
JOE: Sure.

547
00:41:37,892 --> 00:41:41,661
GREG: You know, it's actually headed in the right direction.

548
00:41:41,762 --> 00:41:48,235
Crossing over these sponges, some soft coral, a whole school of small fish

549
00:41:48,335 --> 00:41:51,705
and he is not interested in them.

550
00:41:51,806 --> 00:41:54,475
JOE: And the wind is changing.

551
00:41:54,575 --> 00:41:59,013
NARRATOR: The wind shifts, disturbing the flora in the shallow waters.

552
00:41:59,113 --> 00:42:02,950
and the small prey that live in it.

553
00:42:03,050 --> 00:42:10,724
GREG: Now see this: it's going towards a shallow sandy plain.

554
00:42:10,824 --> 00:42:14,762
Looks like it's going straight for the surface, right? JOE: Yeah!

555
00:42:14,862 --> 00:42:19,467
NARRATOR: The shark's behavior does seem to fit Joe's theory.

556
00:42:19,567 --> 00:42:25,405
The wind brings the smaller fish, and that brings the sharks.

557
00:42:25,505 --> 00:42:28,275
GREG: We know there are smaller fish in the harbor,

558
00:42:28,375 --> 00:42:31,445
I saw some of those when I was down there for a very short time.

559
00:42:31,545 --> 00:42:37,718
JOE: You can actually see the clouds forming right above where he's swimming.

560
00:42:37,818 --> 00:42:40,654
GREG: So you're mixing up their habitats, to maybe,

561
00:42:40,754 --> 00:42:43,858
see what might be happening in them to find possible

562
00:42:43,958 --> 00:42:47,093
food and so eat.

563
00:42:47,194 --> 00:42:51,832
NARRATOR: Joe's crazy idea that shark attacks may be linked

564
00:42:51,932 --> 00:42:57,938
with the weather, it may not be so far-fetched after all.

565
00:42:58,038 --> 00:43:01,708
JOE: It's amazing.

566
00:43:01,808 --> 00:43:07,414
I think coastal winds lead to a food chain response.

567
00:43:07,514 --> 00:43:13,321
which eventually brings a shark close to the shore, where the people are.

568
00:43:17,757 --> 00:43:20,827
GREG: I think there is definitely an influence of weather on behavior.

569
00:43:20,927 --> 00:43:23,831
of the fish beneath the surface.

570
00:43:23,931 --> 00:43:25,932
Perhaps a pattern will emerge and we will predict

571
00:43:26,032 --> 00:43:28,201
the behavior of sharks.

572
00:43:29,436 --> 00:43:34,875
JOE: So that, on a Sunday afternoon, if a family goes to the beach,

573
00:43:34,975 --> 00:43:39,413
can at least get an idea of where the sharks are.

574
00:43:44,352 --> 00:43:47,655
NARRATOR: Meteorologists may soon be able to say:

575
00:43:47,755 --> 00:43:51,158
sunny with strong winds and 80 percent

576
00:43:51,258 --> 00:43:54,662
probability of sharks.

577
00:43:54,762 --> 00:44:01,402
GREG: It's going to take a lot of animals and a lot of information, but I think it's a good start.

578
00:44:01,502 --> 00:44:02,870
JOE: Yes! (laughs)
